title: Trip to jail cell delayed potential treatment
article: Colin Kenson Tremeer, barefoot and standing in the intersection of Highway 97 and Abbott Street, flagged down a passing ambulance, jumped onto the running board, and told a paramedic that someone was trying to kill him.
That was the beginning of the involvement of emergency crews with Tremeer the morning he died, a coroner's inquest heard Tuesday.

Paramedic Jo Ann Hubbard already had a patient she was transporting to Kelowna General Hospital when she encountered Tremeer shortly after 5 a.m. on Aug. 5, so she told Tremeer to get off the ambulance and informed him she would contact the authorities.
Hubbard said she radioed her dispatcher to ask them for police attendance, and continued to the hospital.

The dispatch was relayed to RCMP, and Consts. Jordan McLellan and Dylan Hardy--who had just finished training at RCMP depot a few months earlier--left the RCMP detachment on Doyle Avenue around 5:30 a.m. and began looking for what was described as a "distraught male."
The officers were initially unsuccessful in finding the man and were about to end their patrols when they spotted a man standing in one of the lanes of Highway 97 between Abbott and Water Streets.
Hardy activated his emergency lights, stopped the police vehicle and got out to talk to the man when Tremeer ran around him, opened a back door to the police cruiser and hopped in.
McLellan said Tremeer was "very paranoid," saying that people were trying to kill him.
The officers began asking Tremeer questions to figure out what they were dealing with.
"Due to his agitated state, it was really hard to communicate with him," said McLellan.
They then decided to bring Tremeer back to the RCMP station to figure out what was going on.
"In my mind, there was no better or safer place to gather information" from Tremeer than at the police station, McLellan said.
During the drive back to the detachment, McLellan said Tremeer was flailing, agitated and flushed. He also noticed that the bottoms of Tremeer's feet "appeared to be rubbed off."
He also said Tremeer, who told officers he had taken cocaine, would go in and out of "his own little world" and also believed the RCMP officers were there to harm him.
"We still just tried to calm him down," said McLellan.
After getting into the secure bay at the RCMP station, the officers removed Tremeer from the police car and he began to exhibit "seizure-like" symptoms.
At that point, McLellan thought the situation might be something beyond normal intoxication or mental issues and it might be excited delirium, so he called an ambulance to treat Tremeer.
Officers had to hold down Tremeer's limbs while paramedics first dealt with him and followed the ambulance on the way to the hospital.
Two blocks away from the RCMP station, the ambulance pulled over and Hardy was brought on board to help control Tremeer.
"He was more afraid than anything," said Hardy of Tremeer's flailing.
Police officers were also called to hold Tremeer's limbs when doctors attempted to treat him at the hospital. He died that morning in hospital.

During questioning by Tremeer's father, Ken, McLellan was asked if the fact he was at the end of a shift had any bearing on the decision by officers not to take Tremeer directly to hospital, but McLellan said no.
He later added under further questioning that officers don't normally take people directly to hospital, unless than have been arrested under the Mental Health Act.
He also testified that officers "need to have an evaluation period" to figure out what they are dealing with, and the time it took to take Tremeer to the RCMP station was "lightning fast."
Hardy added he had never dealt with an individual who had excited delirium before, so he had no reason to suspect it.
It wasn't until after the ambulance was called that he thought the symptoms he saw might be excited delirium.
The inquest started earlier in the day with testimony by family and friends of Tremeer, some of whom appeared to be uncomfortable with questions about Tremeer's cocaine and steroid use.
"That's not who he was as a person," said Susanna Hall, who was reticent to answer questions about what sorts of behaviour she saw in Tremeer to indicate he may have been using.
Instead, the mother of Tremeer's son said Tremeer was an "amazing, devoted father" and also described him as the "most ambitious and driven" person she had ever known.

His mother, Marilyn, described the 27-year-old's involvement in many sports, his endless energy, his educational efforts and his dedication to his family, especially to his son, as she read from a prepared statement.

She also made several recommendations for the jury to consider, including that police take people in Tremeer's situation to hospital, not police cells, and asked for training for emergency personnel in excited delirium.
"He (Tremeer) should have been assessed by police and taken to hospital," she said. "A very precious 30 minutes was wasted."
The coroner's inquest is scheduled to conclude today.
